sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension

incidents.title: Remus infostealer reads Gmail through a fake Google Sheets Chrome extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: The Remus infostealer, once on a machine, uses a malicious Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets to read Gmail messages.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The extension works inside the signed-in browser session, so it reads mail without needing the password or MFA. How Remus first reaches the endpoint is not stated in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if an infostealer lands on a laptop where you use Chrome with Gmail; look for a Google Sheets extension you did not install.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An infostealer infection on your Mac or Windows laptop could add the extension to Chrome, which then reads mail from your logged-in Gmail session.
lockItDown: Open chrome://extensions in each Chrome profile and remove any Google Sheets-branded or unfamiliar extension you did not install, especially ones loaded outside the Chrome Web Store.
Open chrome://management and confirm the browser is managed only by your organisation; where you administer Chrome, restrict installs to an extension allowlist.
incidents.roleAngle: A browser extension inherits the user's session, so it defeats MFA; an extension allowlist is the control that matters here.

sources.name: The Record (Recorded Future)
sources.title: Software giant SAP confirms cyber incident amid reports of source code breach

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised

incidents.title: SAP confirms incident; stolen employee GitHub tokens reportedly used to copy and alter code
incidents.evidenceQuote: hackers reportedly used stolen employee tokens to copy and alter source code
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers reportedly used stolen employee GitHub tokens to copy and alter SAP source code.
incidents.realisticRootCause: SAP confirmed an incident and detected suspicious activity on GitHub. The token-theft detail is reported rather than confirmed by SAP, and how the tokens were stolen is not stated.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the same technique works against any GitHub organisation where long-lived personal tokens have broad repository access.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A token taken from a developer laptop, CI log or config file would give an attacker the same read and write access to your repositories as its owner.
lockItDown: In GitHub under Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens, revoke unused tokens and replace classic tokens with fine-grained, expiring ones; also review Settings > Applications for authorised OAuth apps.
In the organisation settings, review the audit log for unusual clone or push activity and require approval for personal access tokens that reach organisation repositories.
incidents.roleAngle: The reported alteration of code, not just copying, makes this a source-integrity issue: branch protection and signed commits matter alongside token hygiene.

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach

incidents.title: 1Password breach: compromised employee GitHub account used to push malicious code
incidents.evidenceQuote: A hacker used a compromised employee GitHub account to push malicious code and steal customer records
incidents.tldrRootCause: An attacker took over an employee's GitHub account, pushed malicious code and reached backend systems holding customer records.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A compromised employee GitHub account was used to push malicious code, which gave access to some backend systems, customer information and internal source code. How the account itself was compromised is not stated; 1Password says vaults and other secrets were not accessed.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the same path exists wherever one developer's GitHub account can push code that reaches production or backend systems.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: If a GitHub account or token in your organisation is taken over, the attacker can push code that your pipelines build and deploy with cloud credentials.
lockItDown: In GitHub organisation settings, check branch protection or rulesets on default branches: require pull request review and block direct and force pushes, including for admins.
Review your GitHub account's Sessions, SSH keys and Personal access tokens pages and revoke anything unrecognised or unused.
incidents.roleAngle: Even a password manager vendor was breached through a single developer account; the control that matters is whether one account alone can ship code to production.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook

incidents.title: SYS01 infostealer enrols browsers in fake management to force a mail-stealing extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management
incidents.tldrRootCause: Malware delivered through Meta ads puts the browser under enterprise-style management and force-installs a data-stealing extension.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A new SYS01 version uses browser management policy to force-install an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook email. The teaser does not say which browsers or operating systems are affected.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes if someone runs a download from a malicious Meta ad; a browser showing as managed when it should not be is the sign.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A download from a malicious ad on a work or personal laptop could put the browser under attacker policy and read webmail sessions used for SSO and account recovery.
lockItDown: Open chrome://management and chrome://policy (or edge://management and edge://policy) and confirm any management or forced-install policy is one your organisation set.
Review the extensions list for anything you did not install or cannot remove.
incidents.roleAngle: Browser policy enrolment is a persistence spot that most endpoint reviews do not look at.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware

incidents.title: PolinRider campaign plants malware in over 7,600 GitHub repositories owned by real developers
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not stated; since the repos belong to real developers, attackers likely pushed with stolen developer credentials or tokens.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The reporting says over 7,600 repositories were compromised, some with a Python loader that fetches next-stage payloads, and that the activity may date back to February 2025. How the developers' accounts or machines were first compromised is not in the excerpt; stolen tokens or an infected developer machine is an inference.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes: your GitHub account or a repo you clone could be affected; look for commits you did not make and unfamiliar loader code in dependencies you pull.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Either your own GitHub credentials are used to push malicious code into your repos, or you clone and run a poisoned repo from a legitimate developer and the loader runs on your laptop.
lockItDown: In GitHub Settings, review the Security log, Sessions, SSH keys and Personal access tokens for anything you do not recognise, and revoke unused tokens.
Review recent commit history on your repos' default branches for pushes you did not make, particularly changes to config or build files.
incidents.roleAngle: The poisoned repos belong to genuine developers, so account age and reputation do not show that a repo is safe.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins

incidents.title: "GoodGuys" phishing uses fake paid expert interviews to steal Google and Okta logins
incidents.evidenceQuote: steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars
incidents.tldrRootCause: Fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars, impersonating major brands, lead victims to hand over corporate Google and Okta credentials.
incidents.realisticRootCause: An ongoing campaign impersonates brands such as Google, Nvidia, Accenture and SpaceX with paid interview or webinar invitations to capture corporate SSO credentials. The teaser does not say how the phishing pages work or whether MFA is bypassed.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes. Security professionals are plausible targets for "paid expert interview" lures, and the campaign goes after Google and Okta SSO logins.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An unsolicited invitation to a paid interview or webinar leads to a sign-in page that captures your corporate Google or Okta credentials, which then open everything behind SSO.
lockItDown: In your Google account security page and your Okta account settings, review recent sign-in activity, active sessions and enrolled MFA factors for anything you do not recognise.
Check that your Google and Okta sign-ins use a phishing-resistant factor (passkey or security key), and treat any interview or webinar invite that asks for a corporate sign-in as suspect.
incidents.roleAngle: A lure aimed at professional vanity and side income; worth a short awareness note to staff who get consulting or expert-network requests.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

incidents.title: NFS2ROOT: 12-year-old Linux kernel NFS server flaw (CVE-2026-99362) allows remote root
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
incidents.attackSurface: Linux kernel NFS server on cloud hosts / K8s nodes
incidents.tldrRootCause: A flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server lets a remote attacker gain root; the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-99362 is a critical, 12-year-old bug in the kernel NFS server component. The teaser does not give the preconditions, affected kernel versions or fix status.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Possibly, if any Linux instance or Kubernetes node in your cloud accounts runs the kernel NFS server and is reachable by untrusted networks.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A Linux VM or node exporting NFS shares, reachable through a permissive security group or firewall rule, could give a remote attacker root on that host.
lockItDown: Review AWS security groups, GCP firewall rules and Azure NSGs for inbound rules allowing the NFS port (TCP 2049) from broad ranges, and narrow them to known clients.
Inventory Linux hosts and K8s nodes that run the kernel NFS server (self-hosted NFS exports, not managed file services) and track your distribution's advisory for CVE-2026-99362.
incidents.roleAngle: Managed file services are a different code path from self-hosted kernel NFS exports; the first job is finding who still runs their own.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Microsoft Store App Found Delivering Vinci RAT Capable of Remote System Control

incidents.title: Fake snipping-tool site uses Microsoft Store app and signed installer to deliver Vinci RAT
incidents.evidenceQuote: begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool
incidents.tldrRootCause: Victims are redirected to a bogus snipping-tool site that serves a Microsoft-signed installer, leading to the Vinci remote access trojan.
incidents.realisticRootCause: According to eSentire, the chain starts with a redirect to a fake snipping-tool site and a Microsoft-signed installer named "Snipping-Tool.exe", using a Microsoft Store application as the delivery vehicle. The excerpt cuts off before the later stages.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, on Windows laptops: a signed, Store-delivered installer for a common utility would pass most casual trust checks.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A user looking for a screenshot tool is redirected to the fake site and runs the signed installer, which gives the attacker remote control of a laptop holding cloud and SSO sessions.
lockItDown: On Windows laptops, look in Settings > Apps > Installed apps and the Downloads folder for an unexpected snipping tool or a file named "Snipping-Tool.exe" that did not come with Windows.
Search DNS or web proxy logs for the fake site domain named in the report (snipp.codes-team[.]com).
incidents.roleAngle: A Microsoft signature and Store origin are not proof of safety; worth checking whether endpoint policy restricts which Store apps users may install.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Most Wanted: The Phishing Kits and Techniques Getting Past Security Controls

incidents.title: Vendor research: phishing kits that most often get past email and web filtering
incidents.evidenceQuote: At Push Security, we measure this as breakthrough rate
incidents.tldrRootCause: No specific compromise; vendor research on phishing kits that evade email security, web gateways and safe browsing.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Push Security ranks phishing kits by how often they get past email security, web gateways and safe browsing to reach the user. The excerpt cuts off before naming kits or techniques.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes in principle: any SSO or GitHub sign-in that accepts a password plus a code or push can be phished if a kit reaches your browser.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A phishing page that gets past filtering reaches your browser and captures your SSO sign-in or session, which then opens cloud consoles and GitHub.
lockItDown: In your identity provider's authentication policy, check whether admin and cloud-console sign-ins require a passkey or FIDO2 key, not push or one-time codes.
Review the authorised OAuth apps and active sessions on your SSO and GitHub account pages and remove any you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: Filtering controls are measurably bypassed, so phishing-resistant sign-in is the control that still holds when a page gets through.

sources.name: CISA KEV (Active Exploitation)
sources.title: CISA KEV: Drupal Core — Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability (CVE-2026-136716)

incidents.title: Drupal core installer flaw (CVE-2026-136716) exploited for unauthenticated site takeover
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to take over a site via the exposed Drupal installer
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers reach an exposed Drupal installer on sites left in an incomplete installation state and take the site over without logging in.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Drupal core does not properly handle unusual or incomplete installation states, so the installer remains reachable and can be abused by an unauthenticated remote attacker. It follows an earlier related flaw, CVE-2026-132165 (Fail2Install), and addresses remaining vulnerable states.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you host Drupal sites; look for Drupal core instances in your cloud accounts with the installer reachable from the internet.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Drupal is not in your stated footprint, so there is no direct path unless a team runs a Drupal site on your cloud infrastructure.
incidents.roleAngle: A second exploited Drupal installer flaw in a short span, on CISA KEV with a 30 November deadline; useful prompt to ask who owns web CMS patching.

sources.name: CISA KEV (Active Exploitation)
sources.title: CISA KEV: OSGeo GeoServer — OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability (CVE-2026-120705)

incidents.title: GeoServer flaws (CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129243) added to CISA KEV; chain gives RCE
incidents.evidenceQuote: via a crafted ID parameter in the WFS 2.0 GetFeatureById stored query
incidents.tldrRootCause: Unauthenticated attackers send crafted WFS requests to GeoServer to read local files or make it fetch URLs, chainable to code execution.
incidents.realisticRootCause: An XML injection in the WFS 2.0 GetFeatureById stored query allows local file reads and server-side requests, and a separate authorisation flaw bypasses service-level role checks via a prefixed service parameter. CISA says these chain with three other CVEs to unauthenticated remote code execution.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you run GeoServer; look for GeoServer containers or VMs with WFS endpoints exposed in your cloud or Kubernetes environments.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: GeoServer is not in your stated footprint; the risk exists only if a data or mapping team has deployed it on your cloud, where the server-side request ability could reach internal services.
incidents.roleAngle: The server-side fetch element matters in cloud settings, since such flaws can be used to reach internal endpoints from a compromised workload.

sources.title: Unpatched Cacti Zero-Day Enables RCE in Just Four HTTP Requests via Guest Access

incidents.title: Unpatched Cacti zero-day with public PoC allows unauthenticated command execution
incidents.evidenceQuote: proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers
incidents.tldrRootCause: A publicly disclosed, unpatched flaw lets an unauthenticated HTTP session reach command execution on Cacti servers via guest access.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The PoC, tracked as 4HTTP2SHELL and 4HTTP2ROOT, reportedly needs four HTTP requests and relies on guest access. No CVE or patch exists yet, and the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.

incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Cacti is not in your stated footprint; a path exists only if a monitoring server in your environment is exposed, where it would give a foothold with network device credentials.
incidents.roleAngle: With a public PoC and no patch, anyone running Cacti has to rely on restricting access rather than on a fix.

incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you or your teams have hex.pm accounts or build Elixir/Erlang projects that pull packages from Hex.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Hex is not in your stated footprint; exposure would be limited to hex.pm account data or API keys if your teams publish or consume Hex packages.
incidents.roleAngle: A reminder that package registries are themselves targets, and that unlogged database reads leave a breach scope unanswerable.

sources.title: GHSA Critical (composer:tastyigniter/tastyigniter): TastyIgniter allows Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Unrestricted file upload in Media Manager

incidents.title: TastyIgniter: admin .htaccess upload in Media Manager leads to RCE (CVE-2026-69179)
incidents.evidenceQuote: Media manager accepts `.htaccess` file which can be used to perform RCE.

incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path through your stated footprint: this is a niche PHP application and exploitation needs admin credentials.

sources.name: GitHub Critical Advisories
sources.title: GHSA Critical (composer:tastyigniter/tastyigniter): TastyIgniter mail template editor allows remote code execution via server-side template injection

incidents.title: TastyIgniter mail template editor allows RCE by admin users via template injection (CVE-2026-69178)
incidents.evidenceQuote: The Mail templates is vulnerable to SSTI and did not perform an validation and sanitization.
incidents.tldrRootCause: An admin with mail template permission can save a template containing PHP that the server then executes.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The mail template body in the admin panel is rendered without validation, so a user with the Admin.MailTemplates permission can inject PHP directives and get code execution when the template is tested. It requires an authenticated admin session; no exploitation in the wild is reported.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you host TastyIgniter; look for the composer package tastyigniter/tastyigniter in any PHP project you run.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path unless you run this restaurant ordering platform, and even then the attacker needs an admin account with mail template rights.
